disclaimer: These cards are general guidance from public agencies. They are not medical advice and do not replace 911 or a professional.

cards.title: Make water safe to drink
cards.summary: Boil if you can. Bleach if you can't.
steps: Boil: a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes above 6,500 feet). Let it cool.
No way to boil: use regular, unscented household bleach (5 to 9 percent). Check the label.
Add 8 drops (about 1/8 teaspoon) per gallon of clear water. Double it for cloudy water.
Stir and wait 30 minutes. It should smell faintly of chlorine. If not, repeat once and wait 15 more minutes.
Bleach older than a year is weaker. Water purification tablets work too; follow the package.
cards.source: CDC, Making Water Safe in an Emergency

cards.title: Is the food still safe?
cards.summary: Keep the doors shut and count the hours.
steps: Fridge: safe for about 4 hours if the door stays closed. After that, throw out meat, poultry, fish, eggs, dairy, cooked leftovers and cut produce.
Freezer: a full freezer holds about 48 hours, half-full about 24, door closed.
Food that still has ice crystals, or is 40°F or colder, can be refrozen or cooked.
Never taste food to check it. When in doubt, throw it out.
Fifty pounds of dry ice keeps an 18-cubic-foot freezer cold for about 2 days. Handle with gloves, ventilate the room.
cards.source: USDA FSIS, Food Safety During a Power Outage

cards.title: Run a generator without hurting anyone
cards.summary: Outside only. Twenty feet from the house.
steps: Outdoors only, at least 20 feet from any door, window or vent, exhaust pointed away. Never in a garage, basement, porch or carport, even with the door open.
Carbon monoxide has no smell. A battery CO alarm inside near the cord is not optional.
Let it cool before refueling. Gasoline on a hot engine is how fires start.
Plug appliances in directly or use a heavy outdoor extension cord. Never plug a generator into a wall outlet.
Headache, dizziness, nausea or confusion: get everyone outside and call 911.

cards.title: The carbon monoxide alarm is going off
cards.summary: Get out first. Ask questions outside.
steps: Get everyone, including pets, outside into fresh air right away.
Call 911 or the fire department from outside.
Do not go back in until responders say it is safe, even if the alarm stops.
If anyone feels sick, dizzy or sleepy, tell the responders. Treatment is oxygen, not fresh air alone.
Common causes in an outage: a generator too close to the house, a grill or camp stove used indoors, a car running in the garage.
cards.source: NFPA and CPSC carbon monoxide guidance

cards.title: Shut off the gas
cards.summary: Only if you smell gas or hear hissing. Then leave it off.
steps: If you smell gas or hear a hiss, leave the house first. Do not flip switches or light anything.
The shutoff valve is on the pipe where gas enters the house, usually by the meter. It has a rectangular tab.
Use a wrench (12-inch adjustable is standard). Turn the tab a quarter turn so it sits across the pipe, not in line with it.
Call the gas company from outside.
Do not turn it back on yourself. Only the utility or a licensed plumber should relight the system.
cards.source: Ready.gov and American Gas Association guidance

cards.title: Shut off the water
cards.summary: Burst pipe, flooding, or when you leave the house in a freeze.
steps: Find the main valve: where the water line enters the house, often near the water heater, in the basement, crawl space or garage, or at the street meter.
Round handle: turn clockwise until it stops. Lever handle: turn a quarter turn so it sits across the pipe.
Open the lowest faucet in the house to drain the lines.
In a freeze with no heat, shutting off the main and draining the pipes can save you a flooded house.
Take a photo of the valve now and keep it in your plan so you are not searching in the dark.

cards.title: Stop serious bleeding
steps: Call 911 or have someone call.
Press hard directly on the wound with a clean cloth or gauze. Do not lift it to look. Add more on top if it soaks through.
If a limb is bleeding heavily and pressure is not working, use a tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound, tighten until the bleeding stops, note the time.
Keep the person warm and lying down. Watch for pale skin, confusion or fainting.
Wash your hands afterward. Small cuts: rinse, press, bandage, watch for redness or swelling over the next days.
cards.source: Stop the Bleed, American College of Surgeons

cards.title: Treat a burn
steps: Cool the burn under cool (not ice) running water for 10 to 20 minutes.
Remove rings and tight things nearby before swelling starts.
Cover loosely with a clean, dry, non-fluffy dressing. Do not pop blisters.
No ice, butter, toothpaste or ointments on a fresh burn.
Call 911 for burns larger than the person's palm, on the face, hands, feet or genitals, from electricity or chemicals, or any burn on a baby.
cards.source: American Red Cross first aid guidance

cards.title: Too hot: heat exhaustion and heat stroke
cards.summary: Cool them down fast. Confusion means 911.
steps: Heavy sweating, weakness, nausea, headache: move to shade or cool air, loosen clothing, sip water, cool with wet cloths and fanning.
Confusion, passing out, hot skin, no sweating, temperature over 103°F: that is heat stroke. Call 911.
While waiting: cool aggressively. Wet the skin, fan, ice packs at neck, armpits and groin.
Do not give fluids to someone who is confused or unconscious.
Check on older neighbors and anyone without air conditioning twice a day in a heat wave.

cards.title: Too cold: hypothermia and frostbite
steps: Shivering, slurred speech, clumsiness, drowsiness: get them somewhere warmer, out of wet clothes, wrapped in blankets. Warm the chest and neck first, not hands and feet.
Warm, sweet drinks if they are awake and alert. No alcohol.
Frostbite (numb, white or gray skin): warm in warm, not hot, water for 20 to 30 minutes. Do not rub. Do not walk on frostbitten feet if it can be avoided.
Severe hypothermia or no shivering: call 911. Handle gently.
In a long freeze: one room, everyone in it, close the doors, blankets over windows. Never heat with the oven or a grill.

cards.title: Flood water
cards.summary: Six inches moves a person. Twelve moves a car.
steps: Never drive or walk through moving water. Turn around.
If water enters the house, turn off electricity at the main panel if you can reach it without standing in water.
Assume flood water is contaminated: sewage, fuel, chemicals. Wash anything it touched. Throw away food it touched, including cans with damaged seals.
Boil-water notices usually follow a flood. Use stored water until the all-clear.
Document damage with photos before you clean up, for insurance.

cards.title: No signal: Emergency SOS on your iPhone
cards.summary: iPhone 14 and later can reach 911 by satellite.
steps: If a call to 911 fails with no cell or Wi-Fi, iPhone 14 and later offers Emergency SOS via satellite. Follow the on-screen prompts.
Go outside with a clear view of the sky. Point the phone where it tells you. Messages take about a minute each.
You can also share your location via satellite in Find My, and text some contacts via satellite on newer iPhones.
Practice the demo once: Settings, Emergency SOS, Try Demo. Do it before you need it.
Keep the phone charged. A dead phone has no satellite.
cards.source: Apple Support, Emergency SOS via satellite

cards.title: Get warnings before and during a storm
cards.summary: Wireless alerts, a weather radio, and two sign-ups.
steps: Wireless Emergency Alerts come to your phone with no app and no account. Keep them on: Settings, Notifications, scroll to the bottom.
Sign up for your county's opt-in alerts (search your county name with "emergency alerts"). These cover evacuations and boil-water notices that national alerts do not.
Register for your utility's outage texts, and ask about a medical program if anyone depends on powered equipment. Some utilities warn those homes first.
Lantern's weather alerts (Settings) check the National Weather Service for the places you save, when the app opens and now and then in the background.
A NOAA Weather Radio with hand crank or batteries is the backup when cell towers go down. Seven frequencies cover the whole country (see Signals).
Program your county into the radio so it only alarms for your area. Keep one by the bed in storm season.
cards.source: FEMA Wireless Emergency Alerts; Ready.gov Make a Plan; NOAA Weather Radio

cards.title: Wildfire smoke: make one clean room
cards.summary: Shut the house, run one filter, stay in one room.
steps: Pick one room with few windows and a door that closes. Everyone sleeps and spends the day there on the worst days.
Close windows and doors. Set air conditioning to recirculate; close the fresh-air intake. Skip the exhaust fan and the gas stove.
Run a portable HEPA air cleaner sized for the room. Filters wear out two to four times faster in smoke; keep spares.
N95 or KN95 masks for trips outside. They do not fit children under two and do not work over beards.
Watch AirNow.gov or the NWS air quality forecast. A hot, smoky day is the hard one: cool the room before you seal it.
Anyone with asthma, heart disease, pregnancy, or over 65 feels smoke first. Have their inhalers and a plan to leave if it gets worse.

cards.title: Refrigerated medicine when the power is out
cards.summary: Keep the door shut. Then a cooler, never on ice.
steps: Leave medicine in the fridge with the door closed. An unopened fridge stays cold for about 4 hours.
After that, move it to a cooler with cold packs. Wrap it in a towel so it never touches ice: freezing ruins insulin and many biologics.
Most insulin keeps for up to 28 days at room temperature once it is out of the fridge; other medicines vary. Read the label or the leaflet. Call the pharmacy if you can.
Do not use insulin that has frozen, looks cloudy when it should be clear, or has clumps.
Red Cross shelters and many pharmacies can refrigerate medicine during a long outage. Ask.
This is general guidance. Your pharmacist or prescriber has the answer for your specific medicine.
cards.source: CDC, Prepare Your Health: Personal Needs; FDA insulin storage guidance
